    10	
    11	Cute DI framework with scopes and agreeable API.
    12	
    13	📚 [Documentation](https://dishka.readthedocs.io)
    14	
    15	### Purpose
    16	
    17	This library is targeting to provide only an IoC-container but tries to make it really useful. 
    18	If you are tired of passing objects manually to create other objects which are only used to create more objects - we have a solution.
    19	Not all projects require an IoC-container, but check what we have.
    20	
    21	Unlike other instruments we are not trying to solve tasks not related to [dependency injection](https://dishka.readthedocs.io/en/latest/di_intro.html).
    22	Instead, we want to keep DI in place, not soiling your code with global variables and additional specifiers scattered everywhere.
    23	
    24	Main ideas:
    25	* **Scopes**. Any object can have lifespan of the whole app, single request or even more fractionally. Many frameworks do not have scopes or have only 2 of them. Here you can have as many scopes as you need.
    26	* **Finalization**. Some dependencies like database connections must not only be created, but carefully released. Many framework lack this essential feature
    27	* **Modular providers**. Instead of creating lots of separate functions or contrariwise a big single class, you can split your factories into several classes, which makes them simpler to reuse.
    28	* **Clean dependencies**. You do not need to add custom markers to the code of dependencies just to allow library to see them. All customization is done within providers code and only the borders of scopes have to deal with library API.
    29	* **Simple API**. You need minimum of objects to start using library. You can easily integrate it with your task framework, examples provided.
    30	* **Speed**. It is fast enough so you do not have to worry about it. It is even faster than many of the analogs.
    31	
    32	See more in [technical requirements](https://dishka.readthedocs.io/en/latest/requirements/technical.html)
    33	
    34	### Quickstart
    35	
    36	1. Install dishka
    37	
    38	```shell
    39	pip install dishka
    40	```
    41	
    42	2. Write your classes, fill type hints. Imagine, you have two classes: Service (kind of business logic) and DAO (kind of data access) and some external api client:
    43	
    44	```python
    45	class DAO(Protocol):
    46	    ...
    47	
    48	class Service:
    49	    def __init__(self, dao: DAO):
    50	        ...
    51	
    52	class DAOImpl(DAO):
    53	    def __init__(self, connection: Connection):
    54	        ...
    55	
    56	class SomeClient:
    57	    ...
    58	```
    59	
    60	4. Create Provider instance. It is only used to setup all factories providing your objects.
    61	
    62	```python
    63	from dishka import Provider
    64	
    65	provider = Provider()
    66	```
    67	
    68	
    69	5. Setup how to provide dependencies.
    70	
    71	We use `scope=Scope.APP` for dependencies which are created only once in application lifetime,
    72	and `scope=Scope.REQUEST` for those which should be recreated for each processing request/event/etc.
    73	To read more about scopes, refer [documentation](https://dishka.readthedocs.io/en/latest/advanced/scopes.html)
    74	
    75	```python
    76	from dishka import Provider, Scope
    77	
    78	service_provider = Provider(scope=Scope.REQUEST)
    79	service_provider.provide(Service)
    80	service_provider.provide(DAOImpl, provides=DAO)
    81	service_provider.provide(SomeClient, scope=Scope.APP)  # override provider scope
    82	```
    83	
    84	To provide connection we might need to write some custom code:
    85	
    86	```python
    87	from dishka import Provider, provide, Scope
    88	
    89	class ConnectionProvider(Provider):
    90	    @provide(scope=Scope.REQUEST)
    91	    def new_connection(self) -> Iterable[Connection]:
    92	        conn = sqlite3.connect()
    93	        yield conn
    94	        conn.close()
    95	```
    96	
    97	6. Create main `Container` instance passing providers, and step into `APP` scope.
    98	
    99	```python
   100	from dishka import make_container
   101	
   102	container = make_container(service_provider, ConnectionProvider())
   103	```
   104	
   105	7. Container holds dependencies cache and is used to retrieve them. Here, you can use `.get` method to access APP-scoped dependencies:
   106	
   107	```python
   108	client = container.get(SomeClient)  # `SomeClient` has Scope.APP, so it is accessible here
   109	client = container.get(SomeClient)  # same instance of `SomeClient`
   110	```
   111	
   112	
   113	8. You can enter and exit `REQUEST` scope multiple times after that using context manager:
   114	
   115	```python
   116	# subcontainer to access more short-living objects
   117	with container() as request_container:
   118	    service = request_container.get(Service)
   119	    service = request_container.get(Service)  # same service instance
   120	# at this point connection will be closed as we exited context manager
   121	
   122	# new subcontainer to have a new lifespan for request processing
   123	with container() as request_container:
   124	    service = request_container.get(Service)  # new service instance
   125	```
   126	
   127	
   128	9. Close container in the end:
   129	
   130	```python
   131	container.close()
   132	```
   133	
   134	10. If you are using supported framework add decorators and middleware for it.
   135	For more details see [integrations doc](https://dishka.readthedocs.io/en/latest/integrations/index.html)
   136	
   137	```python
   138	from dishka.integrations.fastapi import (
   139	    FromDishka, inject, setup_dishka,
   140	)
   141	
   142	@router.get("/")
   143	@inject
   144	async def index(service: FromDishka[Service]) -> str:
   145	    ...
   146	
   147	...
   148	setup_dishka(container, app)
   149	```

   151	### Concepts
   152	
   153	**Dependency** is what you need for some part of your code to work. They are just object which you do not create in place and probably want to replace some day. At least for tests.
   154	Some of them can live while you application is running, others are destroyed and created on each request. Dependencies can depend on other objects, which are their dependencies.
   155	
   156	**Scope** is a lifespan of a dependency. Standard scopes are (without skipped ones):
   157	
   158	  `APP` -> `REQUEST` -> `ACTION` -> `STEP`.
   159	
   160	You decide when to enter and exit them, but it is done one by one. You set a scope for your dependency when you configure how to create it. If the same dependency is requested multiple time within one scope without leaving it, then by default the same instance is returned.
   161	
   162	If you are developing web application, you would enter `APP` scope on startup, and you would `REQUEST` scope in each HTTP-request.
   163	
   164	You can provide your own Scopes class if you are not satisfied with standard flow.
   165	
   166	**Container** is what you use to get your dependency. You just call `.get(SomeType)` and it finds a way to get you an instance of that type. It does not create things itself, but manages their lifecycle and caches. It delegates objects creation to providers which are passed during creation.
   167	
   168	**Provider** is a collection of functions which really provide some objects. 
   169	Provider itself is a class with some attributes and methods. Each of them is either result of `provide`, `alias` or `decorate`. They can be used as provider methods, functions to assign attributes or method decorators.
   170	
   171	`@provide` can be used as a decorator for some method. This method will be called when corresponding dependency has to be created. Name of the method is not important: just check that it is different form other `Provider` attributes. Type hints do matter: they show what this method creates and what does it require. All method parameters are treated as other dependencies and created using container.
   172	
   173	If `provide` is used with some class then that class itself is treated as a factory (`__init__` is analyzed for parameters). But do not forget to assign that call to some attribute otherwise it will be ignored.
   174	
   175	**Component** - is an isolated group of providers within the same container identified by a string. When dependency is requested it is searched only within the same component as its dependant, unless it is declared explicitly.
   176	
   177	This allows you to have multiple parts of application build separately without need to think if the use same types.
